passage: At the anganwadi, Parveen Miss put one coconut ladoo in front of each child. "If you wait until I come back from the kitchen, you get two." Imran stared at his ladoo. His hand crept toward it. Then he sat on both hands, hard. He turned his face to the window and started counting the crows on the wall. "One... two... four..." He hummed the morning rhyme, loudly. The girl beside him licked her ladoo, then ate it. Imran squeezed his eyes shut and kept humming. When Parveen Miss came back, he held up two fingers, grinning. "Two!"

qa.q: What did Imran count while he waited?
qa.a: He counted the crows on the wall.

qa.q: Why did Imran sit on his hands and turn to the window?
qa.a: Imran was tempted and restless, really wanting the ladoo, and keeping his hands and eyes busy helped him wait for two.

qa.q: What could Parveen Miss teach the other children from Imran's tricks?
qa.a: She could show them that looking away, humming or counting something makes waiting easier than staring at the sweet.

qa.q: How might the girl who ate her ladoo feel when Imran gets two?
qa.a: She may feel a little sad or jealous, having found it too hard to stop looking at the ladoo.

grounding: A small boy at the anganwadi sits on his hands and counts crows to wait for a second ladoo.

passage: I'm Sunaina, Nandini's aunt. On Sunday Nani put one gulab jamun on Nandini's plate and said, "If it's still there when I finish my prayer, you get another." I watched from the doorway. Nandini looked at it for a long time. Then she pushed the plate to the far end of the table and turned her chair to face the wall. She started telling her doll a story about a flying elephant. Once she peeked over her shoulder and quickly turned back. When Nani rang the little bell, Nandini spun round. The jamun was still there. I don't know what she was thinking, but she clapped like she'd won a race.

qa.q: What did Nani promise Nandini?
qa.a: If the gulab jamun was still there when Nani finished her prayer, Nandini would get another.

qa.q: Why did Nandini turn her chair to face the wall?
qa.a: She wanted the second jamun, and not seeing the sweet made it easier to wait.

qa.q: Which of Nandini's tricks could help another child wait?
qa.a: Moving the treat away and getting busy with a story, like telling a doll about a flying elephant, takes attention off the sweet.

qa.q: What might Nani feel when she sees the jamun still there?
qa.a: Nani may feel proud and amused that her granddaughter managed to wait, and happy to keep her promise 😊.

grounding: An aunt watches a small girl push away a sweet and tell her doll a story to wait for a second one.

passage:
Monday: Vidya's father, Raghav, set one toffee on the table. "Wait till I finish this call, and you get two." Vidya stared at it, touched it, sniffed it, and ate it in under a minute.
Wednesday: Appa tried again. This time he said, "Want to count the fan blades while you wait?" Vidya counted. Then she sat on her hands and sang her school song, very loudly. She peeked once. She kept singing. When Appa came back, the toffee was still there.
Saturday: Before Appa could say anything, Vidya put the toffee under a cup, turned her back and started building a block tower. "I'm busy," she told it. She got two.

qa.q: What did Vidya do with the toffee on Saturday?
qa.a: She put it under a cup, turned her back and started building a block tower.

qa.q: Why did Vidya sing her school song very loudly on Wednesday?
qa.a: Vidya felt impatient for the toffee, and singing loudly kept her mind off it, so it was easier to keep waiting for two.

qa.q: What change did Raghav make between Monday and Wednesday, and why did it help?
qa.a: He gave her something to do, counting the fan blades, which showed her that distraction makes waiting easier than staring.

qa.q: How might Raghav feel on Saturday when Vidya hides the toffee herself?
qa.a: He may feel proud and amused that she has learned the trick on her own.

grounding: Over a week, a small girl learns to hide the sweet and busy herself so she can wait for two.

passage: The wedding hall was loud and lunch was late. Manjula Aunty put one jalebi on Shreya's leaf. "If it's still there when I come back from greeting the bride, you get two." Shreya stared at the jalebi. Drums boomed, cousins ran past, and Aunty took a long time. Shreya sat on her hands. She turned her whole body toward the band and counted the drummers aloud, "One, two, three, four!" Then she counted balloons. When Manjula Aunty came back, the jalebi was still there, sticky from the heat. "Two!" Shreya shouted, holding up two fingers.

qa.q: What did Shreya count first while she waited?
qa.a: She counted the drummers aloud.

qa.q: Why did Shreya turn her whole body toward the band?
qa.a: She wanted the second jalebi, and not seeing the sweet made the wait easier; looking at the drummers kept her hands and mind busy.

qa.q: Which part of Shreya's waiting worked best, and why?
qa.a: Counting drummers and balloons; thinking about something else carried her through the long, noisy delay better than staring at the jalebi and trying hard.

qa.q: How might Manjula Aunty feel on coming back to the leaf?
qa.a: Manjula Aunty finds an untouched jalebi and a proud child holding up two fingers, and is likely delighted that Shreya waited so long in all that noise 😊

grounding: A young child sits on her hands and counts drummers to avoid eating a sweet so she can earn two.

passage: In the Kolkata flat, Vijay's mother, Sarita, put one sandesh on a steel plate. "I'm hanging the washing. Wait till I'm done and you get two." Vijay knelt by the table, nose almost touching the plate. He licked his lips. Then he pushed the plate behind the fruit bowl and ran to the window. "Tram!" he called. He sang the bus song twice, loudly, and hopped on one foot. When Sarita came back with the empty bucket, Vijay was on the floor making a train out of slippers. "Did you forget the sweet?" she asked. "No," he said. "I hid it from me."

qa.q: Where did Vijay push the plate?
qa.a: He pushed the plate behind the fruit bowl.

qa.q: What does 'I hid it from me' suggest about what Vijay was thinking?
qa.a: He knew that seeing the sandesh made waiting hard, so he wanted it out of sight and his mind on trams, songs and slippers.

qa.q: What could Sarita offer next time to make the wait easier from the start?
qa.a: She could suggest a song or a slipper train as soon as she sets the sweet down, and put the plate out of sight herself.

qa.q: How might Sarita feel hearing 'I hid it from me'?
qa.a: Sarita may be amused and quietly proud that her little boy found his own trick for waiting while she was busy with the washing.

grounding: A young child hides a sweet and busies himself with songs and play so he can earn a second one.

passage: On the veranda of their village house, Harsha Didi put one laddoo on a steel plate in front of Mridul. 'If you wait till I come back from the well, you get two.' She left. Mridul stared at the laddoo. He licked his lips. Then he sat on his hands, hard. He turned around and watched the goats. He counted them, twice. He sang the rain song under his breath. When Harsha Didi came back with the pot on her hip, the laddoo was still there. Mridul held up two fingers, grinning.

qa.q: Where did Harsha Didi go?
qa.a: She went to the well.

qa.q: Why did Mridul sit on his hands and count the goats?
qa.a: He really wanted the laddoo, and keeping busy helped him feel less tempted so he could wait for two.

qa.q: What helped Mridul wait more than just trying hard?
qa.a: Distracting himself, sitting on his hands, turning away, counting goats and singing, took his mind off the laddoo.

qa.q: How might Harsha Didi feel seeing the laddoo still there?
qa.a: She would likely feel pleased and proud of him.

grounding: A young child sits on his hands and looks away from a laddoo to earn two, using distraction rather than raw willpower.

passage: In the kitchen in Leeds, Daniel put one chocolate biscuit on a plate in front of Layla. 'I need to finish a phone call. If the biscuit is still here when I'm done, you can have two.' He stepped into the hallway. Layla looked at the biscuit. She touched it with one finger. Then she pulled her hand back and covered her eyes. She turned her chair to face the window and told the pigeons on the fence a long story about a dragon. When Daniel came back, the biscuit was still there, with one small fingerprint on it. 'Two!' Layla shouted.

qa.q: Which way did Layla turn her chair?
qa.a: She turned it to face the window.

qa.q: Why did Layla cover her eyes?
qa.a: She wanted the biscuit badly, and not seeing it helped her feel less tempted.

qa.q: What did Layla do that helped her wait?
qa.a: She covered her eyes, turned away and told the pigeons a story, which kept her mind off the biscuit.

qa.q: What might Daniel think seeing the fingerprint?
qa.a: He might feel amused, knowing she was tempted but still managed to wait.

grounding: A young child waits for a second biscuit by covering her eyes and telling a story, using distraction rather than willpower.

passage: At the preschool, Amandeep Sir held up the sticker sheet. 'One sticker now, or two after the story. You choose.' Most of the children grabbed one. Bhavna looked at the shiny star stickers for a long time. Then she said, 'Two.' During the story she kept glancing at the sheet on the table. So she sat on her hands, then lay down on the mat and watched the ceiling fan going round and round. When the story ended, she jumped up. 'Now two!' Amandeep Sir gave her two stars, and she stuck them on her cheeks.

qa.q: What did Bhavna watch to stop glancing at the stickers?
qa.a: She watched the ceiling fan going round and round.

qa.q: Why did Bhavna keep glancing at the sticker sheet?
qa.a: She really wanted the shiny stars, so waiting felt hard and tempting.

qa.q: What helped Bhavna wait for two stickers?
qa.a: Sitting on her hands and lying down to watch the ceiling fan distracted her from the stickers.

qa.q: How might Amandeep Sir feel when Bhavna asks for her two stars?
qa.a: He would likely feel pleased and amused, especially when she sticks them on her cheeks.

grounding: A young child waits for two stickers by sitting on her hands and watching the fan, using distraction to delay.

passage:
Before (a hot April day): Samir Bhaiya put one jalebi on a plate. “Wait till I come back, Anirban, and you get two.” Anirban stared at it. He ate it in ten seconds.
During (a week later): Same jalebi, same plate. This time Anirban turned his chair to face the wall and hummed a song about a train. He sat on his hands. He counted his toes.
After (the next Sunday): Samir came back. The jalebi was still there.
“Two!” Anirban shouted, clapping. He ate both slowly, licking the syrup off his fingers.

qa.q: How long did it take Anirban to eat the jalebi the first time?
qa.a: He ate it in ten seconds.

qa.q: How did Anirban feel when he got two jalebis?
qa.a: He felt proud and delighted, shouting and clapping.

qa.q: What helped Anirban wait the second time?
qa.a: Turning away, humming a song, sitting on his hands and counting toes: distractions that made waiting easier than plain willpower.

qa.q: How might Samir Bhaiya feel seeing the jalebi still there?
qa.a: Samir Bhaiya probably felt surprised and proud of his little brother.

grounding: The three beats show a young child learning to wait for a second sweet by looking away and distracting himself.

passage:
On Eid, Farida Khala's house was loud with cousins and clattering plates.
Khala put a piece of kaju barfi in front of Vandana. “If you can wait until I finish serving, you'll get two.”
Vandana, five, looked at the barfi. It was shiny.
She sat on her hands. She watched the cousins' game. She sang “Chanda mama door ke” under her breath.
A cousin shouted. The barfi was still there. Vandana squeezed her eyes shut.
Khala came back. “Still there? Shabaash!” She added a second piece.
Vandana giggled and ate one. She saved the other for later.

qa.q: What sweet did Khala put in front of Vandana?
qa.a: A piece of kaju barfi.

qa.q: How did Vandana feel when Khala added a second piece?
qa.a: She felt proud and happy, giggling with delight.

qa.q: Which tricks helped Vandana wait in the noisy house?
qa.a: Sitting on her hands, watching the cousins' game, singing and closing her eyes, distractions that did more than raw willpower.

qa.q: How might Farida Khala feel seeing the barfi still there?
qa.a: Khala likely felt pleased and impressed, saying “Shabaash!”

grounding: The passage shows a young child during a noisy Eid gathering waiting for a second sweet by distracting herself.

passage:
On Diwali evening, crackers popped everywhere. Pallavi Maasi put one kaju katli on a steel plate. “Neelam, if you don't eat it till I light the diyas, you get two.”
Neelam, four, sat on the balcony step with the plate beside her. She looked at the sweet. She looked away.
She counted the diyas as Maasi lit them. She lost count and started again. A rocket shot up.
She sat on her hands.
When Maasi lit the last diya, Neelam jumped up. “I didn't eat it!”
“Two for you,” said Maasi.
Neelam held one sweet in each hand, beaming.

qa.q: What did Neelam count while she waited?
qa.a: She counted the diyas as Maasi lit them.

qa.q: How did Neelam feel when she jumped up?
qa.a: She felt excited and proud that she hadn't eaten the sweet.

qa.q: What helped Neelam wait?
qa.a: Counting diyas, watching rockets and sitting on her hands kept her mind off the sweet.

qa.q: How might Pallavi Maasi feel watching Neelam beam with two sweets?
qa.a: Maasi probably feels happy and proud of Neelam's patience.

grounding: The passage shows a young child at Diwali waiting for a second sweet by looking away and counting diyas.

passage:
It was Diwali evening, and the laddoos sat on the steel plate by the diyas.
"Vaibhav," said Swati Masi, "you can have one laddoo now. Or, if you wait till the pooja is over, you get two."
"Two!" Vaibhav said. "I can wait."
He sat on the floor. He looked at the laddoos. He licked his lips.
"Masi, is it over?"
"Not yet."
Vaibhav sat on his hands. Then he turned round to face the window. "I'm counting diyas. One, two, three..."
"How many?"
"Eleven! And the neighbour has a big rocket."
When the bell rang, he spun round. "Now two?"
Swati Masi put two on his palm.

qa.q: What did Swati Masi offer Vaibhav if he waited till the pooja was over?
qa.a: She offered him two laddoos.

qa.q: How can you tell Vaibhav really wanted the laddoo while he waited?
qa.a: He looked at the laddoos and licked his lips and kept asking if it was over, which shows he felt eager and impatient.

qa.q: Which of Vaibhav's tricks helped him wait, and why?
qa.a: Sitting on his hands and turning to count diyas took his mind and eyes off the laddoos, which is easier than just trying hard not to eat them.

qa.q: How might Swati Masi feel when she gives Vaibhav two laddoos?
qa.a: She probably feels pleased and proud of him, and glad she kept her word.

grounding: It shows a child sitting on his hands and looking away to count diyas so he can wait for two sweets instead of one.

passage:
Class teacher's note, KG-B, Christmas week — Charu
We baked star cookies for the party. The children could eat one now, or two after the carols.
Varun chose two. He stared at the tray, then covered his eyes with both hands. Next he hummed very loudly, off-key. Then he went to the block corner and built a tall tower with his back to the tray.
After the carols, I gave Varun his two cookies and said I noticed how he waited. He grinned and broke one in half for his friend.
Next week I will teach the class the humming and turning-away trick as a game. 🎄

qa.q: What did Varun build in the block corner?
qa.a: He built a tall tower with his back to the tray.

qa.q: Why did Varun cover his eyes and hum loudly?
qa.a: He felt tempted and eager for the cookies and was trying hard to stay patient, so he hid them from his eyes and filled his head with the song.

qa.q: What does the teacher plan to do next, and why is it useful?
qa.a: The teacher plans to teach the humming and turning-away trick as a game, so other children learn that distraction helps more than just trying hard.

qa.q: How might Varun's friend feel getting half a cookie?
qa.a: The friend would feel happy and surprised to share in Varun's reward.

grounding: It shows, through a teacher's note, a child covering his eyes, humming and turning away to wait for two cookies instead of one.

passage:
At the Sankranti mela in the village, the jalebi man fried spirals in a black pan.
"One jalebi now," said Gargi Phuppo, "or two when the bus comes to take us home."
"Two," Farida decided.
The smell was strong. Farida turned her back to the pan. She watched the kites over the field. She counted the cows by the pond. She made up a song about a buffalo with a hat.
"Phuppo, bus?"
"Not yet."
She sang the buffalo song again, louder.
At last the bus honked, and Farida got two jalebis, one for each hand.

qa.q: What did Farida count by the pond?
qa.a: She counted the cows by the pond.

qa.q: How was Farida feeling while she waited for the bus?
qa.a: She felt tempted and impatient, because the jalebi smell was strong and she kept asking about the bus.

qa.q: What helped Farida wait, and what could other children copy?
qa.a: Turning her back to the pan and watching kites, counting cows and singing a silly song kept her busy; other children could copy the same distracting games.

qa.q: What is it like for Gargi Phuppo to watch Farida wait?
qa.a: Gargi Phuppo probably feels fond and amused, watching Farida sing about a buffalo with a hat to keep from asking.

grounding: It shows a child turning away from the sweets and distracting herself with kites, cows and a song so she can wait for two jalebis.

passage:
At the Kuala Lumpur kindergarten the Lunar New Year lanterns were up, and Cikgu Fatima put one pineapple tart in front of Mei. "If you can wait till I come back from the office, you get two."
Mei stared at the tart. She licked her lips. Then she sat on her hands, turned her whole chair to face the window, and sang the lantern song, loud, swinging her feet. She counted the red lanterns. One, two, three, four...
When Cikgu Fatima came back, the tart was still there. Mei's face lit up. "Two!"

qa.q: What did Cikgu Fatima put in front of Mei?
qa.a: One pineapple tart.

qa.q: How was Mei feeling while she stared at the tart?
qa.a: Mei wanted it badly and felt tempted, since she licked her lips, and then happy and proud when she earned two. 😊

qa.q: Which of Mei's tricks worked, and why?
qa.a: Sitting on her hands, turning to the window, singing and counting lanterns; keeping her mind busy elsewhere helped more than just trying hard not to eat it.

qa.q: What would change if Mei had to keep staring at the tart?
qa.a: The wait would likely feel much harder and she might have eaten it; looking away made waiting bearable.

grounding: A young child sits on her hands, looks away and sings to earn a second sweet, using distraction rather than raw willpower.
